tour.title: A Hillside Village Above Ephesus
tour.summary: An evening in a Greek Orthodox hill village that became Turkish in 1923 — two restored churches, lanes of stone-and-timber houses, wine houses pouring sweet fruit wines, and the valley going gold at dusk.
tour.overviewText:
Şirince looks, at first glance, like a Greek island that lost its sea: white walls, dark timber, red tiles, shutters, and lanes too narrow for anything but feet. It sits at about 330 metres on a hillside above the Aegean plain, eight kilometres east of the market town of Selçuk and a short drive from the ruins of Ephesus. You have come up here for the evening, and the village rewards that: by late afternoon the day-trippers drain away, the stone gives back the day's heat, and the light goes gold across the valley.

The village's whole story is written in its walls, and it begins with a religion. For centuries this was a Greek Orthodox community — the Ottomans called such Christians Rum, from "Roman", meaning the Greek-speaking Orthodox heirs of Byzantium — and by the nineteenth century it was a prosperous town of well over a thousand households that grew rich on figs, tobacco, olives and wine, and built the tall stone-and-timber houses and the two Orthodox churches you will walk past. Their mother tongue, oddly, was Turkish; they prayed in Greek and counted in Turkish. Then came 1923. Under the Treaty of Lausanne, Greece and Turkey agreed to exchange their religious minorities: roughly 1.2 million Greek Orthodox Christians left Turkey for Greece, and some 355,000 to 400,000 Muslims left Greece for Turkey. Şirince's Greek families went to Greece, many founding the village of Nea Efesos near Katerini; Turkish-speaking Muslim families from the Kavala region of northern Greece were settled in their houses. The old village did not vanish — it changed hands. The churches were left standing, the houses were reoccupied, and the wine terraces were worked by people who had never grown grapes.

The walk is short and steep. It starts at the edge of the village where the road from Selçuk ends, follows the main lane of stone houses down to the larger of the two Orthodox churches, climbs back through the market street where the wine houses pour their tastings, then up a hillside lane for the view over the valley and the second church, and finishes in the little square as the lights come on.

Everything on this walk is free to enter: the village, both churches, the viewpoint. The centre is car-free, so park or get dropped at the edge. The cobbles are steep and polished — wear shoes with grip, especially after rain. A dolmuş — a shared minibus that leaves when it fills — runs up from Selçuk's bus station every twenty to thirty minutes and takes about fifteen minutes; pay the driver in cash, in Turkish lira (₺). The route itself is about a kilometre and a half, roughly twenty minutes of walking; give it two hours with the churches, the tastings and the dusk.

Come for the churches and the wine, but stay for the thing the day-trippers miss: a real village of a few hundred people, going quiet for the night.
tour.difficulty: Easy to moderate. Short, but steep and uneven: polished cobbled lanes with steps between terraces, no step-free route. Wear shoes with grip, especially after rain.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Late afternoon into evening. Arrive by about 5pm so both churches and the wine houses are open, climb to the upper village for the hour before sunset, and finish in the square as the lights come on. Mornings are quieter but the light over the valley is an evening show.

stops.name: Village Entrance and Main Street
stops.narration:
The road up from Selçuk ends here, at the edge of the village, and this is where cars stop. The lanes ahead are too narrow for them — the centre is car-free, so from now on you are on foot, on cobbles, going downhill into the village.

Start with the name, because it is a small lesson in how places change hands. The village was Kırkınca, or in Greek Kirkintzes, and the name is usually traced to the Turkish word kırk — forty. The story goes that forty people, or forty families, came up into these hills in some legendary age and gave the place its name. There is a competing folk tale that runaway slaves called it Çirkince, "ugly", to keep others away; it is a good story and a doubtful one. What is certain is that in 1926, three years after the new Turkish Republic was founded, the governor of İzmir ordered the name changed to Şirince, "pleasant" or "charming" — a small act of rebranding that stuck.

Now look at the houses, because they explain the village. The ground floor is stone, cut from these hills; the upper floor is timber-framed, plastered and whitewashed, with a wide overhang, wooden shutters and a red-tiled roof. This is a style you also find in the Balkans — some historians trace it to settlers who came here from southern Albania in the eighteenth century. The lanes were laid out so that no house blocks another's view, and the terraces step down the hill in rows.

Who lives here now? A few hundred people, most of them farming — olives, peaches, some grapes — or working in the guesthouses and restaurants that have grown up around tourism. The tall houses you are walking between were mostly built in the nineteenth century, when this was a rich Greek Orthodox town; the people who live in them today are the descendants of the Muslim families who were settled here in 1923. Keep that in mind as you walk down — the next stop explains what happened.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk the village. If you drive up, edge-of-village parking costs a small fee in ₺ — verify at the car park, as rates move.
stops.openingHours: The village is always open. Shops and wine houses generally run from mid-morning to around 20:00 or later in summer; hours shrink out of season.
stops.accessibility: Honestly hard: steep, uneven, polished cobbles with steps between levels. There is no step-free route through the village; the entrance lane itself is the easiest stretch.
stops.insiderTip: Leave the main street. Two lanes up or down and the shops give way to gardens, cats and people going about their day — that is the real village.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the entrance, walk down the main lane into the village, past the stone houses, following the signs for the churches. The Church of St John the Baptist is about four hundred metres downhill, on the left, the big building on a terrace above the lane.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Erik Cleves Kristensen, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Church of St John the Baptist
stops.narration:
This is the Church of St John the Baptist — in Turkish, Aziz Yahya Kilisesi — and it is the biggest building in the village. It was built in 1805, probably on the site of an older church destroyed in an earthquake in 1800, with help from a Greek benefactor, Kallinikos of Siphnos; Siphnos is a Greek island, which tells you how the Orthodox world of the Aegean was knitted together across borders. An inscription over the door dated 1832 records a second repair.

It is Greek Orthodox. Before 1923 this village was entirely Christian, and its people were what the Ottoman Empire called Rum — the Greek Orthodox subjects of the sultan, who mostly spoke Greek in church and, here, Turkish at home. The church was their centre: three naves divided by columns, two domes, a half-dome over the apse, cut stone outside and timber beams within. Walk in and look up. The western dome collapsed at some point and was rebuilt in restoration; in the niches of the apse you can still make out faded frescoes of saints. The nave is bare and quiet now — no icons, no liturgy — because this has not been a working church for a century.

That century began in 1923. After the Greco-Turkish war, Greece and Turkey signed the Treaty of Lausanne and agreed to a compulsory exchange of minorities, defined by religion rather than language. Roughly 1.2 million Greek Orthodox Christians were uprooted from what is now Türkiye and sent to Greece; roughly 355,000 to 400,000 Muslims were sent from Greece to Türkiye. Şirince's Greek families left for Greece, and many of their descendants founded a new village, Nea Efesos, near Katerini in the north. Into their houses came Turkish-speaking Muslim families from Moustheni and Domatia, two villages in the Kavala region of northern Greece. Each side lost a homeland and gained a stranger's. The exchange was brutal, and it was agreed by both governments; it is the single event that made this village what it is. Same streets, same houses, same church — different people.

The church fell out of use and stood empty for decades, until the Ephesus Museum and the American Institute restored it in the 1990s. Today it stands in the garden of a private property and is free to enter. It is a monument now, not a place of worship, so treat it like one: quiet, no touching the frescoes, and a coin in the wishing well by the door — there is a statue of the Virgin Mary over it — if you want the local custom. Then walk back up toward the market street; the wine houses are a couple of minutes uphill.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free entry. The church stands in the garden of a private property and depends on goodwill and donations; leave a coin at the wishing well if you wish.
stops.openingHours: Generally open in daylight hours, but it stands in a private garden and can be locked. If the gate is shut, admire the exterior and the wishing well and come back later — verify on the day.
stops.accessibility: A step or two into the church and a stone-paved narthex; the interior floor is level once inside. The lane up to it is steep cobbles.
stops.insiderTip: Look up at the apse niches for the faded frescoes — most visitors photograph the dome and miss the painting. The collapsed west dome you see was rebuilt in the 1990s restoration.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the church, climb back up the lane toward the market street, then follow Çarşı Sokağı east. The wine houses line the street within a few minutes' walk; look for the bottles in the doorways.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Kadı, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Wine Houses and the Vine Terraces
stops.narration:
These lanes are the village's larder and its cash register. Şirince is famous across Türkiye for wine, and the shops you are walking past are the reason: almost every other doorway is a şaraphane, a wine house, with bottles lined up like sweets and someone behind the counter holding out a small glass.

Understand the drink first. Alongside ordinary grape wines, the village makes fruit wines — blackberry, mulberry, peach, apple, melon, pomegranate, strawberry — and most of them are sweet, closer to a dessert wine than to the dry red you might expect. They are not a gimmick; they are what the hills grow. Look around and you can see the raw material: the slopes above and below the village are terraced with bağ — vineyards — mixed with olive groves and peach orchards. A terrace, if you have not thought about it, is a flat strip cut into a slope and held up by a low stone wall; on a hill like this it is the only way to farm without the soil washing away, and the walls you see between the vines are centuries of that work.

The wine is old here, and the interruption is the interesting part. In the nineteenth century this was a rich town whose money came from figs, tobacco, olives and wine. After 1923, the Greek families who had made that wine left, and the Muslim families who replaced them came from the Kavala region of northern Greece, which grew tobacco, not grapes. For a generation the vineyards were neglected and the wine trade faded; the village grew poor, and by the 1950s families were drifting down to Selçuk. The revival came late — the road was paved in the 1980s, restorers began saving the old houses, and tourism brought the wine back. What you are tasting is an old tradition that was nearly lost and has been rebuilt for visitors.

Tasting is easy and buying is easy. Almost every shop will let you try before you commit; treat it as a shop, not a free bar, and buy a bottle if you have tasted. Prices are in Turkish lira and rise with inflation, so ask. Cash is preferred in the small stalls. And if you are flying, remember that bottles travel best in checked luggage, wrapped in clothes. When you have had enough, climb the lane on the far side of the market street toward the upper village; the second church and the best view are up there.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk the street. Tastings are usually free if you buy a bottle, otherwise expect a modest charge; bottles run from a few hundred ₺ upward — ask, because prices move with inflation and shops differ.
stops.openingHours: Wine houses are usually open from mid-morning until around 20:00, later in summer; hours vary shop by shop. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: The market street is a narrow cobbled lane with gentle steps, and wine-house doorways usually have a step. Not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Ask for a taste before you buy — the shops expect it — and try a fruit wine you have never heard of, like myrtle or melon. It is sweet: think dessert, not dinner.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the wine houses, take the lane climbing uphill on the far side of the market street, toward the upper village. Follow the signs for the second church — about four hundred metres, steep, and the view opens as you climb.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Chansey, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Hillside Lane and the Valley View
stops.narration:
You have climbed to the top of the village, and this is the reward. Below you the rooftops step down the hill in rows of red tile; beyond them the ground falls away into olive groves and the long valley that runs west toward Selçuk and the Aegean. On a clear evening the light comes in low and sideways, and you can see why the villagers built up here: cool air, defensible ground, and a view of anyone coming.

The building beside you is the second of the village's two Orthodox churches, the Church of St Demetrios — Agios Dimitrios, a soldier-saint much loved in the Orthodox world. It is smaller than St John the Baptist and, to many people, finer. Step inside if it is open: the carved and painted wooden screen at the front — the iconostasis, the panel of icons that separates the congregation from the altar in an Orthodox church — is the most beautiful thing in Şirince, painted in blue, red and gold. Like its neighbour it was built by the Greek community and left behind in 1923, then restored in recent decades; entry is free, and there is a small café next to it.

One custom from this church ties the whole region together. Until 1923, on 15 August, the Feast of the Assumption — the day Orthodox and Catholic Christians mark the Virgin Mary's ascent into heaven — the villagers set out from here on a five-hour walk to the House of the Virgin Mary, the shrine above Ephesus. The walk ended; the shrine did not. It is now a place of pilgrimage for both Christians and Muslims, and you can still visit it, twenty minutes down the hill.

Look at the valley while you are up here, because it explains Ephesus. Two thousand years ago the sea came almost to the foot of this hill: Ephesus was a great port, and this slope was its hinterland, supplying it with water through the Roman aqueducts whose broken arches still stand beside the road up. Then the Küçük Menderes river silted the gulf, the coast retreated about fifteen kilometres west to Kuşadası, and the port died. Şirince outlived it — a hill village does not need a harbour.

Stay for the light if you can. The sun sets over the valley to the west, and the hour before it goes is the best in the village. When you are ready, walk back down into the square; it is a few minutes downhill, and that is where the evening happens.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free: the lane, the porch and the view cost nothing. Entry to the Church of St Demetrios is free too.
stops.openingHours: Open access — the lane and the view are always there. The church may be locked outside daylight hours; verify locally.
stops.accessibility: The climb is steep and stepped, and the lane is cobbled and slippery when wet. The church porch and the view are reached by the same uphill lane — no step-free route.
stops.insiderTip: The hour before sunset is the best light in the village. Bring a layer: at 330 metres the hill is noticeably cooler than the coast after dark.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the upper lane, walk back down into the village centre; the square with the mosque and the plane tree is about three hundred and fifty metres below you, easy to find by the minaret.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Lastradadeisogni, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Village Square at Dusk
stops.narration:
This is the village square — a small open space with a plane tree, a fountain, café tables and the mosque on one side. It is where Şirince meets itself: children, cats, old men, and the day's visitors deciding whether to stay for dinner. In the evening, when the tour buses have gone back down the hill, it belongs to the village again.

Notice what is around you, because each thing is a layer of the story you have been walking through. The mosque marks the change: a Greek Orthodox town became a Muslim one, and a Muslim congregation now prays where the village's Orthodox Christians once did. Five times a day the ezan — the call to prayer, sung from the minaret — goes out over the rooftops, a sound you will hear across Türkiye. The market street nearby sells what the village actually makes: olives and olive oil, olive-oil soap, honey, jams, pomegranate sauce, pekmez — a thick syrup boiled down from grapes or mulberries — strings of dried peppers and aubergines, and handmade lace. It is a good place to buy something real, and cash is preferred.

If you are hungry, look for gözleme: a thin flatbread, rolled out and cooked on a griddle in front of you, filled with cheese, spinach or potato. Turkish families drive up from İzmir and Selçuk at weekends for a long village breakfast, and the restaurants on the edge of the village have terraces looking out over the valley.

One last, strange chapter. In December 2012, when a New Age reading of the Mayan calendar predicted the end of the world, Şirince was named as one of the safe places on Earth — supposedly charged with "positive energy". Crowds of believers, journalists and police came up the hill to wait for the apocalypse. The apocalypse did not arrive; the village did, and it has been a fixture of Turkish day-trip tourism ever since. You can decide what that says about the place.

That is the walk. You began among the stone houses of a Greek Orthodox town and ended in the square of a Turkish one, in the same streets, a hundred years apart. If you have the morning free, the obvious pairing is back down the hill: Ephesus at opening time, before the heat, and the Ephesus Museum in Selçuk, where the statues and finds from these hills are kept. Şirince will still be here when you come back.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to wander. Food, drinks and market goods are at village prices; small stalls prefer cash in ₺.
stops.openingHours: Open at all hours. Liveliest from late afternoon into the evening, when the day-trippers have gone.
stops.accessibility: The square is the most level place in the village, but the lanes into it are cobbled and stepped.
stops.insiderTip: Stay for dinner after the day-trippers leave. The village goes quiet, the square lights up, and the restaurants on the edge have valley views.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. The dolmuş back to Selçuk leaves from the edge of the village — ask at a shop or your guesthouse for the current times, because the last one goes in the evening and after that it is a taxi (agree the fare first). If you are staying the night, the square empties after dark and the village is at its best. And keep Ephesus and the Ephesus Museum in Selçuk for the morning: they are fifteen minutes down the road and worth the early start.
